articles.title: Enhancing Efficiency and Quality in Thyroid Biopsy: The Long-Term Impact of Implementation of a Program of Dedicated Sonographer-Performed Thyroid Biopsies.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the long-term diagnostic performance and consistency of a dedicated sonographer-performed thyroid FNAB program under radiologist supervision. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective quality improvement study (QIRC 23-0591) analyzed consecutive thyroid FNABs performed between 2008 and 2022 at a single academic center. A structured sonographer training program was implemented in 2011. Biopsies were categorized into three periods: pre-implementation (2008-April 2011), early post-implementation (August 2011-2013), and late post-implementation (2014-2022). FNABs performed by other clinicians during the late implementation period served as a contemporaneous control group. Outcomes were assessed at the nodule level using the Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology. Trend analyses were performed using the Cochran-Armitage test; chi-square tests compared groups. RESULTS: A total of 14,127 thyroid nodules were biopsied in the radiology (4,382 pre-implementation; 2,561 early post-implementation; 7,184 late post-implementation period). Nondiagnostic rates decreased from 34% (1492/4382) pre-implementation to 21% (534/2561) early post-implementation and 8.6% (617/7184) late post-implementation period (p<.001). Malignant cytology increased from 4.9% to 5.6% to 7.7%, and combined Bethesda V/VI diagnoses increased from 8.9% to 8.5% to 12.1% (both p<.001). During late post-implementation period, sonographer-performed FNABs demonstrated lower nondiagnostic rates (8.6% vs 29%, p<.001) and higher malignant yield (7.6% vs 4.5%, p<.001) compared with other clinicians. Adoption of ACR TI-RADS in 2020 was not associated with significant changes in adequacy or malignancy rates. CONCLUSIONS: A dedicated sonographer-performed thyroid FNAB program improved diagnostic adequacy and malignancy yield over 11 years, supporting safe delegation of thyroid FNAB to trained physician extenders under radiologist supervision.

articles.title: PaSTA: Fast parametric inference of significance for spatial associations between brain maps.
articles.abstract: Testing for spatial correlations between pairs of brain maps has emerged as a central task in neuroimaging studies. Determining the statistical significance of such correlations is challenging due to the presence of spatial autocorrelation in brain maps. Here we establish a novel parametric method, Parametric Spatial Test for Associations (PaSTA), to infer the significance of spatial associations between brain maps via covariance-variance modelling and effective degrees of freedom estimation. Our method is fast, reliable, and sensitive, enabling flexible significance testing of brain map correlations over arbitrary cortical surface and brain volumetric domains. We examine the sensitivity and specificity of PaSTA using simulated datasets with known ground truth and demonstrate its utility when applied to empirical brain maps. We extend PaSTA to approximately model modest nonstationarity in spatial autocorrelation and show that, our method yields improved false positive control and statistical power relative to existing approaches when brain maps are spatially heterogeneous.

articles.title: Masked Position Modeling as a Pre-Training Strategy for Foundational Deformable Image Registration Models.
articles.abstract: The core objective of deformable image registration (DIR), estimating a displacement vector field that aligns two images, is fundamentally the same across imaging modalities and anatomical regions. Although this shared objective should imply the use of foundation models, most deep learning approaches for DIR operate within narrow domain-specific settings. Vision Transformers (ViTs) are the predominant choice for foundation models in many image processing tasks due to their excellent generalization capabilities and robustness to domain shifts. However, their use remains largely underexplored for DIR, which we attribute to a lack of suitable pre-training schemes. To address this need, we introduce MPM-Reg, a transferable, modality-agnostic training paradigm based on masked position modeling (MPM), enabling the use of fully transformer-based models as foundation models for image registration. Unlike conventional masked data modeling, which predicts the content of masked image patches, MPM masks the positional information and predicts the spatial relationship between image patches. Initially, we employ MPM on single images, which naturally aligns self-supervised pre-training of ViTs with the downstream registration task. Subsequently, we extend MPM to predict the positions of target patches within source images, re-formulating DIR through the lens of MPM. Experiments across eleven diverse datasets demonstrate MPM-Reg's competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Crucially, MPM-Reg benefits from heterogeneous multi-domain data, which degrades the performance of existing methods, paving the way for scalable foundation models for DIR.

articles.title: Beyond Landmark Error: Agreement Between AI-Assisted and Manual Cephalometric Tracing at the Level of Clinical Measurements: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence has revolutionized the field of dentistry. This systematic review evaluated the clinical performance of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cephalometric tracing compared with manual or expert digital tracing. Methods: We searched the PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science databases from inception to 20 May 2026. Studies directly comparing AI-assisted tracing with manual or expert digital tracing of the same lateral cephalograms and reporting at least one clinically relevant cephalometric outcome were included in the review. Two authors independently screened records. Risk of bias was assessed using an adapted QUADAS-2 framework. A quantitative meta-analysis was planned but not performed. Findings were synthesised narratively by measurement, platform, and workflow, with reporting informed by the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) guideline. Results: Twenty studies were included. Direct AI-versus-reference ICCs were reported in more than three studies, but their formulations and reference procedures varied. Small average differences sometimes coexisted with wide individual limits of agreement. The numerical evidence did not establish a consistent ranking of SNA, SNB, and ANB. Conclusions: AI-assisted tracing may be useful as a clinician-verified adjunct, but its performance depends on the measurement, platform, and workflow. The evidence does not establish uniform clinical interchangeability with manual or expert digital tracing.

articles.title: Arteriovenous Malformations as Neoplastic-Like Lesions: Molecular Underpinnings and Implications for the Interventional Radiologist.
articles.abstract: Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) are high-flow vascular anomalies traditionally treated as congenital structural lesions with embolization or surgical resection. However, recurrence after embolization alone exceeds 90%, underscoring incomplete understanding of their biology. Next-generation sequencing has identified somatic gain-of-function mutations in KRAS, MAP2K1, BRAF, and HRAS as drivers of sporadic AVMs. Confined to lesional endothelial cells, these mutations activate RAS/MAPK signaling and support a neoplastic-like rather than purely structural disease model. This has therapeutic implications: MEK inhibitors, particularly trametinib, have shown angiographic and clinical responses in refractory AVMs. Interventional radiologists can obtain draining vein liquid-biopsy samples during embolization for molecular genotyping; embolization may increase circulating cell-free DNA yield. This review summarizes the molecular rationale, targeted therapy evidence, and integration of genotyping into embolization workflows to enable combined treatment strategies.Level of Evidence: No level of evidence assigned (Review Article).

articles.title: Pancreatic mucinous cystic neoplasms in adults: An update on the role of CT and MRI for risk stratification.
articles.abstract: Pancreatic mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCNs) are characterized histologically by an inner mucin-producing columnar epithelium supported by a dense ovarian-type stroma. MCNs account for approximately 10% of pancreatic cystic neoplasms. Surgical resection is the treatment of choice, as MCNs may harbor high-grade dysplasia or progress to invasive carcinoma. Establishing reliable imaging criteria for risk stratification is critical to identify patients who are candidates for surgery. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging play pivotal roles in lesion characterization and assessment of features associated with high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma. Current guidelines recognize several imaging features as high-risk characteristics for MCNs, including large tumor size, mural nodules, and main pancreatic duct dilatation. However, other potential predictors of malignancy remain poorly defined and are not sufficiently emphasized. The strongest MCN-specific evidence, as demonstrated in multivariable analyses, supports larger cyst size, mural nodules, main pancreatic duct dilatation, and, in selected cohorts, elevated serum cancer antigen 19-9. Male sex has also been associated with malignancy in retrospective surgical cohorts, whereas pancreatic head/neck location, calcification, wall/septal thickening, age, and signal heterogeneity on T2-weighted images remain less consistently validated. Importantly, most malignancy-prediction literature is based on resected, pathologically confirmed MCNs and is therefore vulnerable to selection and verification bias and cannot be directly extrapolated to all incidentally detected presumed MCNs. This article presents a transparent literature search methodology and an evidence-based synthesis of predictors of malignancy that clearly distinguishes MCN-specific multivariable evidence from lower-level or extrapolated data. It also provides a comparison of key guidelines. Unlike previous reviews, this article directly addresses the evidence gap between resection-based cohorts and the broader population of incidentally detected presumed MCNs. It also clarifies when imaging findings should prompt further evaluation rather than independently determine management.

articles.title: Explainable vision transformer framework for breast lesion classification with Grad-CAM support.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Given that breast cancer remains the most lethal malignancy among women globally, there is an urgent need for reliable and comprehensible diagnostic technology. Deep learning models have demonstrated encouraging outcomes in breast imaging; nevertheless, existing methodologies struggle to encompass global context and deliver clinically relevant justifications for their conclusions. METHOD: The ExViT-Breast framework was trained and internally validated on CBIS-DDSM (n = 1,566 subjects; masses and calcifications), externally validated on INbreast, and evaluated across modalities on the BUSI ultrasound dataset. A Vision Transformer backbone with a cross-view attention fusion module integrated paired craniocaudal (CC) and mediolateral oblique (MLO) mammographic views. Four explainability methods were compared: Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, LayerCAM, and Transformer-LRP. Classification performance was assessed by AUC and sensitivity at one false positive per examination. Explanation quality was evaluated using faithfulness (deletion/insertion curves), clinical plausibility (pointing game against expert-defined lesion regions), and ensemble-based uncertainty estimation. Model calibration was quantified using Expected Calibration Error (ECE). RESULTS: ExViT-Breast achieved superior diagnostic performance with an AUC of 0.94 ± 0.02 on CBIS-DDSM, significantly outperforming conventional CNN architectures (ResNet-50: AUC = 0.89, p < 0.001) and single-view Vision Transformers (AUC = 0.91, p = 0.003). External validation on INbreast demonstrated robust generalization (AUC = 0.91 ± 0.03), while cross-modality evaluation on BUSI yielded AUC = 0.88 ± 0.04. Transformer-LRP consistently provided the highest explanation quality across all datasets, achieving faithfulness scores of 0.71 ± 0.05 and plausibility rates of 79.5% on CBIS-DDSM, significantly superior to Grad-CAM variants (p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: The ExViT-Breast framework demonstrates the potential of explainable Vision Transformers in breast imaging, combining high classification performance with clinically interpretable explanations. The integration of multi-view analysis and quantitative explainability assessment positions this approach as a promising tool for computer-aided diagnosis in breast cancer screening and detection. CLINICAL TRIAL: Clinical trial number: not applicable.

articles.title: Adaptive Liver Stiffness Quantification in Magnetic Resonance Elastography Using a Heterogeneity-Aware Deep Learning Framework.
articles.abstract: Magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) enables non-invasive liver stiffness measurement (LSM). However, accurate quantification remains operator-dependent particularly for identifying clinically valid measurement regions and selecting a representative sampling strategy. This study developed and validated a fully automated, heterogeneity-aware deep learning framework that integrates valid-region identification, elastogram heterogeneity assessment, and a study-specific adaptive quantification strategy, while substantially reducing analysis time. The framework was evaluated in a prospective cohort of 201 subjects. Magnitude images and wave-attenuation images were combined to identify valid regions for LSM. Because spatial stiffness heterogeneity may increase sensitivity to region-of-interest (ROI) placement, elastograms were classified as homogeneous or heterogeneous using a multimodal convolutional neural network-deep neural network (CNN-DNN) classifier that integrates spatial image features with quantitative stiffness descriptors. For homogeneous elastograms, a study-specific distributed circular-ROI reduced-sampling strategy was evaluated, whereas volumetric sampling was applied to heterogeneous elastograms to better capture spatial variations in stiffness. The segmentation module achieved a Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.894 ± 0.035, an Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.810 ± 0.057, and a 95th-percentile Hausdorff-Distance (HD95) of 5.45 ± 4.05 mm. Automated LSMs showed excellent agreement with expert measurements (ICC = 0.998; Bland-Altman bias = 0.007 kPa), while reducing analysis time from approximately 15 min to 0.35 s/patient. The heterogeneity classifier achieved accuracies of 89.4% and 88.5% at the slice and patient-levels, with areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) of 0.928 and 0.935, respectively, demonstrating substantial patient-level agreement with the expert reference classification (Cohen's κ = 0.770). By integrating automated valid-region identification with objective elastogram heterogeneity assessment, the framework may improve standardization and reproducibility of LSM.

articles.title: Blank-Image Ablations Can Mislead: A Mismatched-Image Control for Visual-Requirement Audits in Medical-VQA-Evidence from ERA-TurkMed, A Turkish Generative System.
articles.abstract: Whether a Medical Visual Question Answering (Medical-VQA) system uses its image is usually tested by replacing it with a zero tensor: if performance does not drop, the image is deemed unused. We show that this test can mislead. We built ERA-TurkMed, to our knowledge the first generative Medical-VQA system for Turkish radiology (frozen BiomedCLIP, Q-Former, LoRA-adapted Llama-3.1-8B), trained by a three-stage curriculum on a single-center, ethics-approved dataset (~ 5000 chest radiographs; ~ 17,476 question-answer pairs). On the full test set (n = 3454, three seeds), BLEU-4 is higher without the image (Δ =  - 0.024 ± 0.007, seed-level p = 0.025). A mismatched-image control-an in-distribution radiograph of a different patient-reverses this conclusion: the real image is better on polarity accuracy (+ 0.035, p = 0.030), chrF (+ 0.018, p = 0.020), and exact match (+ 0.015, p = 0.028) in all three seeds. The blank-image advantage is confined to the BLEU family and the hallucination rate, and reverses on polarity accuracy, a measure validated against manual annotation (95.0% agreement) that exposes the negation blindness of clinical-term F1. The visual contribution is nonetheless small: 77.2% of test questions recur verbatim in training, and an image-free retrieval baseline matches the model on clinical-term F1 (0.496 vs. 0.510), a consequence of template-based, AI-assisted dataset construction rather than of Turkish. We therefore recommend verbatim-overlap auditing, an image-free baseline, a mismatched-image control, and negation-sensitive metrics as standard. Code is available; model weights follow upon publication. The clinical data cannot be shared under Turkish data-protection law (KVKK).

articles.title: Deep Learning Radiomics to Predict Vessels Encapsulating Tumor Clusters and Prognosis in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Based on Gd-EOB-DTPA-Enhanced MRI.
articles.abstract: Vessels encapsulating tumor clusters (VETC) are significantly associated with poor prognosis in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), with implications for patient survival and clinical management. This study aimed to evaluate a deep learning (DL) radiomics model based on Gd-EOB-DTPA-enhanced MRI for preoperative prediction of the VETC pattern in HCC. Patients with pathologically confirmed HCC who underwent Gd-EOB-DTPA-enhanced MRI between January 2016 and August 2024 were retrospectively enrolled. Visually assessed radiological features were collected to construct a clinical-radiological (CR) model. Deep learning and handcrafted radiomics features were extracted from arterial, portal venous, and hepatobiliary phases. Feature selection and DL radiomics model construction were performed using the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO). Multivariable logistic regression was applied to develop a hybrid model and corresponding nomogram. Model discrimination was quantified using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Cox regression analysis was performed to identify predictors of recurrence-free survival (RFS). In the training cohort, the hybrid DL-radiomics nomogram yielded the highest AUC (0.92), compared with 0.87 for the DL model, 0.80 for the radiomics model, and 0.74 for the CR model. However, standalone DL model showed better discriminative performance in the internal validation cohort, with an AUC of 0.87, sensitivity of 0.80, and specificity of 0.87. VETC status, AST level, and intratumoral necrosis were identified as independent predictors of RFS and incorporated into the VAI prognostic model. The VAI model achieved an AUC of 0.75 (95% CI, 0.68-0.80), which was significantly higher than those of three conventional prognostic systems (range, 0.52 [95% CI, 0.46-0.59] to 0.58 [95% CI, 0.51-0.64]). The hybrid DL-radiomics model based on Gd-EOB-DTPA-enhanced MRI showed favorable discriminative performance for VETC prediction in the training cohort, while the standalone DL model demonstrated better performance in the internal validation cohort. The VAI model enables individualized prediction of postoperative RFS for patients undergoing hepatectomy.

articles.title: Auditing Report Order in Emergency Teleradiology Using Routine Event Logs.
articles.abstract: This study aims to describe recorded report-order inversions in emergency teleradiology and assess their interpretation when assignment and active interpretation times are unavailable. We reconstructed computed tomography (CT) transmissions from July 2025 through June 2026, requiring a unique exact linkage and stable priorities. An inversion occurred when a later examination received its first recorded report before an earlier examination still unresolved at the same provider. Eligible head-abdomen pairs were analyzed using dependence-preserving intervals, an empirical conditional reference and secondary models incorporating retrieved imaging workload proxies. Among 8170 examinations, 6,051 had the standard ED urgent category. Later head CT inverted 1060/1761 earlier-abdomen pairs (60.2%; 95% confidence interval, 57.5-62.7%); later abdominal CT inverted 154/1038 earlier-head pairs (14.8%; 12.3-17.5%). Observed-minus-reference differences were - 4.5 percentage points (- 7.3 to - 1.6) and - 11.4 (- 14.2 to - 8.8). Counts were usable for 3474/3565 target examinations and 2665 pairs. Report-order asymmetry did not demonstrate preferential dispatch. Observed inversion proportions were below the empirical conditional reference probabilities. This does not establish protective scheduling. Routine exports support a descriptive audit; additional workflow events are necessary to identify mechanisms or compare dispatch policies.

articles.title: Predicting Findings from Radiology Indication Text: BERT vs Naïve Bayes Classification.
articles.abstract: This retrospective study evaluated Naïve Bayes (NB) and transformer-based BERT models for predicting findings from radiology order Indication text for use in radiology informatics and automated worklist triage systems. From the MIMIC-CXR-JPG dataset, 219,995 chest radiograph orders were extracted, and the indication text was paired with CheXpert-generated labels for a binary (findings/none) and multi-label (13-category) classification task. Three BERT models (baseBERT, radBERT, BioClinicalBERT) were compared to NB classifiers using bootstrap confidence intervals, McNemar's test, and paired permutation tests. Precision-recall curves assessed triage utility under a high-precision constraint. On the binary task, all BERT models significantly outperformed NB on AUROC (0.793-0.798 vs. 0.763; P < 0.001  ). The radBERT model did better on AUROC than baseBERT and BioClinicalBERT (0.798 vs. 0.793 for both; P < 0.001  , DeLong test) by a small but statistically significant amount. On the multi-label task, NB had better micro-F1 at the default threshold (0.399 vs. 0.361-0.388; P < 0.001  ), but the BERT models had better AUPRC (0.470-0.475 vs. 0.358) and calibration (expected calibration error 0.011-0.016 vs. 0.077). NB's apparent advantage was due to its overconfident probabilities, not overall superiority. At a 90% precision constraint, radBERT recalled 55.0% of positive orders (36,557 examinations triaged per 100,000 annual orders). At 95% precision, radBERT maintained an actionable recall of 26.4%, whereas NB's recall collapsed to near zero. The modest edge of radBERT over general-domain and clinical-note-pretrained variants on the binary task suggests the distinctive character of Indication text limits the benefit of domain-specific pretraining. Order Indication text contains actionable information for predicting imaging findings, supporting transformer-based models for automated radiography triage systems.

articles.title: Postdeployment Performance of a Commercial Artificial Intelligence System for Pulmonary Nodule Detection at Chest CT: Examination-Level Agreement, Clinical Indication, and Image-Based Review Across 13,536 Examinations.
articles.abstract: Postdeployment performance of pulmonary nodule detection AI is rarely measured. This retrospective, cross-sectional analysis of prospectively collected routine data evaluated a commercial detection system (ClearRead CT; Riverain Technologies), deployed with a candidate-size threshold of greater than 3 mm, across 13,536 consecutive chest CT examinations at one academic center (January 2025-January 2026). Final reports, classified by natural language processing (NLP; validated against manual review of 896 reports: sensitivity 99.5%, specificity 99.6%, κ 0.99), served as the examination-level comparator; randomly selected discordant examinations were reviewed on images. Because radiologists viewed AI output before reporting, report-referenced results are presented as agreement; accuracy estimates are given only after image review. AI was positive in 9142 examinations (67.5%) and reports documented a nodule in 3919 (29.0%). Positive percent agreement was 80.6% (95% CI 79.4, 81.8), negative percent agreement 37.8%, and report-referenced positive predictive value 34.6%; 5982 examinations (44.2%) were AI positive/report negative, and Cohen κ was 0.13 (maximum attainable, 0.33). Agreement was 98.6% for screening, 38.3% for oncologic, and 32.6% for inpatient/emergency examinations, which contributed 76.1% of discordance. On image review, 291 of 298 (97.7%) AI-positive/report-negative examinations contained only non-nodule structures, and 196 of 198 (99.0%) AI-negative/report-positive examinations contained an unmarked nodule larger than 3 mm, 45 of them (23.0%) larger than 6 mm. Review-adjusted examination-level sensitivity was 81.2%, specificity 38.2%, and positive predictive value 35.4%. These findings describe one configuration at one institution; performance should be measured locally, by indication, and against image review.

articles.title: Prediction of Double-Expressor Lymphoma in Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma Using a Non-invasive Model Based on [18F] FDG PET/CT and Stacking.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: To develop and validate an interpretable multimodal model integrating deep learning radiomics with clinical data using baseline [18F] FDG PET/CT for non-invasive identification of the double-expressor lymphoma (DEL) in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). MATERIALS AND METHODS: The histopathological reference standard for DLBCL diagnosis and DEL subtyping was immunohistochemistry according to the 2016 WHO. Patients from January 2019 to July 2025 were retrospectively enrolled and randomly divided into training and test sets at 7:3, and a patient-level analysis was performed. Clinical, radiomics and deep learning features were extracted. After LASSO selection, individual and fusion models were constructed. Statistical analyses were performed using Python (3.6), and p-value < 0.05 was considered significant. Model performance was assessed via receiver operating characteristic (ROC), calibration and decision curve analysis (DCA). SHAP and a nomogram were used for interpretation. RESULTS: A total of 143 patients (82 males, 61 females, median age 61.5 years) were enrolled. ViT_KNN model achieved a test AUC of 0.936 (95%Cl 0.856-1.000), outperforming clinical (AUC 0.857, 95%Cl 0.722-0.993) and radiomics (AUC 0.706, 95%Cl 0.547-0.865) models. Late fusion, especially Stacking_LR, achieved the best performance (AUC 0.948, 95%Cl 0.865-1.000, accuracy 95.3%, specificity 100%, sensitivity 88.2%). Calibration and DCA confirmed clinical net benefit. SHAP analysis highlighted deep learning features as most influential. The Stacking_LR nomogram offers an intuitive clinical tool. CONCLUSION: Deep learning radiomics based on baseline [18F] FDG PET/CT enables effective non-invasive identification of DEL. The stacking ensemble strategy enhances multimodal fusion and provides a highly accurate, interpretable tool for DLBCL risk stratification.

articles.title: Sex-Related Multivariate Organization of Glymphatic MRI Markers in Healthy Adults.
articles.abstract: Sex may influence MRI-derived markers related to brain fluid and perivascular processes, but sex differences across glymphatic-related MRI markers remain unclear. We investigated sex differences in individual and multivariate glymphatic-related MRI markers in healthy adults. The Human Connectome Project (HCP) was used as the discovery dataset (n = 971; 521 females), and the Chinese Human Connectome Project (CHCP) was used as an independent validation dataset (n = 307; 157 females), from which a range of glymphatic-related MRI markers was derived. Sex differences in these glymphatic-related markers were examined, followed by principal component analysis (PCA) to characterize their multivariate organization. We found that males showed higher choroid plexus volume fraction, perivascular space volume fraction, and white-matter free-water fraction, but lower values for the index of diffusivity along the perivascular space and the index of periventricular diffusivity than females. PCA identified two dominant components explaining 63.45% of the total variance. Most glymphatic-related MRI markers showed consistent sex-related patterns in CHCP, and sex differences in HCP-projected component scores were directionally consistent with HCP. PCA performed separately in HCP and CHCP showed high similarity of the retained two-dimensional subspaces, with differences in individual component loading patterns. Together, these findings characterize sex-related variation in glymphatic-related MRI phenotypes at the individual-marker and multivariate levels.

articles.title: Development and external validation of a CT-based clinicoradiological model for preoperative differentiation of pancreatic adenosquamous carcinoma from ductal adenocarcinoma.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To develop and externally validate a CT-based clinicoradiological model for preoperative differentiation of pancreatic adenosquamous carcinoma (PASC) from pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). MATERIALS AND METHODS: This dual-center retrospective study included 397 patients with surgically confirmed PASC or PDAC and preoperative contrast-enhanced CT. In the development cohort, patients with PASC were matched 1:2 to patients with PDAC by age, sex, and tumor location. At the second center, consecutive eligible patients with PASC and PDAC identified during prespecified diagnosis-specific study periods constituted the external validation cohort. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression followed by multivariable logistic regression was used for model development. RESULTS: In the development cohort, the integrated model achieved an AUC of 0.919. In the external cohort, discrimination was preserved (AUC, 0.846; 95% CI, 0.781-0.910), but calibration was poor (slope, 0.445; 95% CI, 0.309-0.603). Calibration-in-the-large was 0.152 (95% CI, -0.358 to 0.656), with an observed-to-expected ratio of 1.03. The integrated model outperformed the clinical-only model (ΔAUC, 0.179; p < 0.001), whereas incremental discrimination beyond the imaging-only model was not demonstrated (ΔAUC, -0.004; p = 0.85). Decision curve analysis in the development cohort suggested potential net benefit across selected threshold probabilities. CONCLUSION: The CT-based clinicoradiological model showed good external discrimination but substantial miscalibration, supporting its potential for preoperative risk stratification rather than individual probability estimation. Further recalibration and prospective validation in unselected, prevalence-representative populations are required before clinical use.

articles.title: Standardized shear wave elastography of ex vivo lymph nodes: a multistage evaluation of platform configurations, quality control, and reproducibility.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: Ex vivo lymph node (LN) shear wave elastography (SWE) enables mechanical phenotyping, but measurements depend on specimen support, coupling, loading, and platform configuration. We aimed to establish and evaluate a standardized acquisition and quality-control (QC) framework. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This prospective, single-center, ex vivo methodological study included 141 LNs from 20 surgical patients in four non-overlapping cohorts. We compared water-tank coupling-pad (WT-CP) with water-tank nylon-mesh (WT-NM; n = 24), then compared the selected WT-CP configuration with gel-cup (GC) and sandwich coupling-pad (SCP; n = 36), and finally compared selected WT-CP with SCP in a final-stage paired comparison (n = 46). An independent cohort assessed reproducibility (n = 35). Outcomes included feasibility, QC burden, within-LN coefficient of variation (CV%), mean elasticity (Emean), confidence, and operator agreement. RESULTS: WT-NM yielded lower Central and Whole-LN ROI Emean than WT-CP (both P < 0.001) without improving Central ROI CV% (P = 0.119). In platform screening, LN-level PASS was 36/36 for selected WT-CP, 31/36 for GC, and 35/36 for SCP; GC had the greatest QC burden. In the final-stage paired comparison, LN-level PASS was 46/46 for selected WT-CP and 45/46 for SCP. Central ROI CV% was 4.14 % versus 3.67 % (P = 0.761), whereas Emean was 17.02 versus 20.30 kPa (P < 0.001). Interoperator ICC(A,1), based on three-acquisition averaged measurements, was 0.900 for Central ROI and 0.915 for Whole-LN ROI (mean bias, 0.49 kPa; limits of agreement, -2.95 to 3.93 kPa). Intraoperator ICC(A,1) ranged from 0.946 to 0.963. CONCLUSION: Platform configuration affected feasibility, QC burden, and the absolute Emean scale; absolute values from different configurations should not be assumed interchangeable.

articles.title: Charge collection efficiency in air-vented plane-parallel ionisation chambers at ultra-high dose rates: a self-consistent Garfield++ Monte Carlo model including space-charge effects and ion recombination.
articles.abstract: Ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) irradiation used in FLASH radiotherapy can lead to significant reductions in charge collection efficiency (CCE) in plane-parallel ionisation chambers (PPICs) due to enhanced ion recombination, while the high charge densities involved can also induce strong space-charge-induced electric-field distortions. This work aims to develop a Monte Carlo framework for investigating these coupled effects.Approach: We extended the Garfield++ Monte Carlo particle-transport framework by implementing ion-ion recombination and self-consistent space-charge electric field calculations. The resulting model couples particle transport, electron attachment, recombination processes, and dynamic electric-field distortions. The implementation was validated against analytical and numerical models from the literature.Main results: Excellent agreement was obtained for the free electron fraction (FEF), CCE, induced current, and electric field evolution under UHDR conditions. The simulations show that space charge can locally increase the electric field by more than a factor of four or reduce it to nearly zero in some regions of the chamber. The results further suggest that the decrease in the FEF caused by electric-field-dependent electron attachment plays a major role in the reduction of the CCE under UHDR conditions.Significance: These findings highlight the importance of accurately describing the evolution of the FEF for modelling recombination under UHDR conditions, opening up prospects for improved analytical models and real-time correction methods for ionisation chamber dosimetry. More broadly, this work provides a flexible and self-consistent Monte Carlo framework for investigating recombination phenomena and improving dosimetry models for FLASH radiotherapy.

articles.title: Giant Wilms tumor in a 5-year-old boy.
Intraarticular acetabular osteoid osteoma treated with CT-guided radiofrequency ablation after unsuccessful arthroscopy: a case report and literature review.
articles.abstract: Acetabular osteoid osteoma is uncommon, and treatment can be difficult when the lesion is intraarticular or associated with osteoarthritis. We report a 17-year-old male with an intraarticular acetabular osteoid osteoma. The lesion was located in the medial portion of the acetabular fossa and was associated with synovitis, joint effusion, joint space narrowing, and osteophyte formation. Arthroscopy was initially selected for lesion resection and joint assessment. However, the medial location limited instrument access, preventing complete resection. The residual lesion was subsequently treated with CT-guided radiofrequency ablation (RFA) using a posterior osseous trajectory and intraarticular cooling with chilled 5% dextrose solution. At 4 weeks, hip pain had completely resolved, and MRI showed resolution of perilesional bone marrow edema. Pain relief persisted through 12 months without analgesic use. A literature review summarizes previous treatment approaches for acetabular osteoid osteoma. This case illustrates that treatment planning should account for lesion location, joint condition, and technical feasibility. CT-guided RFA may be useful when a safe percutaneous trajectory to the lesion can be planned.

articles.title: Comparative Diagnostic Accuracy of Image-Guided Aspiration Techniques for Periprosthetic Hip Infection: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Image-guided fluid aspiration is a key component in the diagnostic work-up of suspected prosthetic joint infection of the hip (PJI). Fluoroscopy, ultrasound (US), and computed tomography (CT) are frequently employed to guide aspiration; however, comparative evidence regarding their diagnostic performance and procedural outcomes remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate and compare the diagnostic accuracy and technical performance of these modalities. METHODS: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL were searched for studies evaluating fluoroscopy-, US-, or CT-guided hip aspiration to aid PJI diagnosis. Outcomes of interest included diagnostic performance, dry tap rates, and procedural characteristics. Dry tap rates were pooled by modality using random-effects meta-analysis of proportions. Due to heterogeneity in reference standards, diagnostic accuracy outcomes were synthesised narratively. RESULTS: Ten studies comprising 1,574 hip aspirations were included (647 fluoroscopy, 831 US, 96 CT). Sensitivity ranged from 0.52-0.89 for US and 0.27-0.83 for fluoroscopy, with consistently high specificity (≥0.75) across modalities. CT-guided aspiration demonstrated sensitivity of 0.67 and specificity of 0.98 in a single study. Pooled dry tap rates were lower for US (17%, 95% CI 4-30%) compared with fluoroscopy (27%, 95% CI 9-45%), with substantial heterogeneity (I²>97%). CONCLUSIONS: Reported specificity is comparable between ultrasound- and fluoroscopy-guided hip aspiration for PJI. Ultrasound-guided aspiration demonstrates higher reported sensitivity and lower dry tap rates, although interpretation is limited by heterogeneity in reference standards. ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: This review provides a focused synthesis of comparative evidence on imaging modalities for hip aspiration in PJI. It highlights a potential diagnostic and practical advantage of ultrasound-guided aspiration.

articles.title: Assessment of Glucose Metabolism in Vivo in the Human Frontal Lobe Using Interleaved 1H and 13C MRS at 7T.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: 13C magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS), combined with 13C-labeled substrate infusion, offers a nonionizing, minimally invasive method for assessing fluxes through the main cerebral energy metabolism pathways. However, its human application at 7T has not been fully established, especially within the frontal lobe, where alterations are linked to various neurological and psychiatric disorders. PURPOSE: To explore the feasibility of the interleaved 1H/13C MRS protocol for quantification of cerebral glucose uptake and downstream metabolism at 7T, and to estimate the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle flux (VTCA) for validation. STUDY TYPE: Prospective. POPULATION: Three healthy volunteers (Two females and one male). FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: 7T; single voxel spectroscopy: ACE-STEAM (indirect 1H-[13C]) and ISIS-DEPT (direct 13C-[1H]). ASSESSMENT: ACE-STEAM and ISIS-DEPT were applied to acquire the time-resolved spectra in the frontal lobe. 13C-labeled glucose, glutamate, and glutamine fractional enrichment time courses were quantified to estimate VTCA through the one-compartment model. STATISTICAL TESTS: The relative estimated fitting uncertainties (EFUs) were reported for the processed spectra. Nonlinear least squares minimization was used for flux fitting of 13C traces. Uncertainty of the estimated metabolic fluxes was evaluated using Monte Carlo simulations. RESULTS: [1-13C]-glucose (GlcC1) was detected within 6 min on 13C MR spectra, followed by 13C-labeled GluH4 and GlnH4, and then GlxH3 can be quantified on 1H MR spectra. End-of-infusion mean enrichments were 17% (GluH4), 13% (GlnH4), and 7% (GlxH3). Brain glucose concentration ranged 1.86-2.94 mM, with 61% of the mean enrichment in C1. Group-average VTCA was 0.66 ± 0.07 μmol/g/min (n = 3). DATA CONCLUSION: This interleaved 1H/13C MRS protocol, combined with 13C-labeled glucose infusion, enables minimally invasive quantification of cerebral metabolic fluxes. As a proof-of-concept feasibility study in a small healthy volunteer cohort, it may provide a useful framework for investigating neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases at 7T. EVIDENCE LEVEL: 1. TECHNICAL EFFICACY: Stage 1.

articles.title: Three-Dimensional Phase-Contrast MR Angiography at 5 T Assesses Warming-Associated Changes in the Visible Hand Vascular Network in Systemic Sclerosis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Thermal challenge can reveal vascular abnormalities in systemic sclerosis (SSc), but current assessments primarily measure surface temperature or cutaneous perfusion. Warming-associated changes in the visible three-dimensional hand vascular network in SSc remain incompletely characterized. PURPOSE: To quantify warming-associated changes and group differences in hand-size-normalized metrics of visible hand vessels using 5-T three-dimensional phase-contrast MR angiography (3D PC-MRA), and to assess repeatability and reader agreement. STUDY TYPE: Prospective case-control study. POPULATION: Ninety participants (60 SSc, mean age: 44.00 ± 10.73 years, 55 females; 30 healthy controls, mean age: 42.83 ± 13.24 years old, 28 females). Twenty controls (18 females) underwent baseline scan-rescan imaging; reader agreement was assessed in the 60 baseline examinations. FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: 5 T; noncontrast-enhanced 3D gradient-echo PC-MRA. ASSESSMENT: Hands were imaged before and after 5-min immersion in 40°C water. Hand-size-normalized metrics were vessel volume (nVol), centerline length (nLen), and apparent vessel radius (nRad); changes (Δ) were post-immersion minus baseline. STATISTICAL TESTS: Paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests; Welch t-tests; multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, and baseline values; intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs); and Bland-Altman analysis. Significance was q < 0.05 after Benjamini-Hochberg correction and p < 0.05 otherwise. RESULTS: Normalized vessel volume and normalized centerline length increased significantly in both groups, with mean changes of 0.76 × 10-3 and 1.91 in controls and 1.80 × 10-3 and 4.80 in SSc, respectively. Adjusted increases were significantly greater in SSc for normalized vessel volume (between-group difference, 1.11 × 10-3; 95% CI, [0.36-1.85] × 10-3) and normalized centerline length (difference, 1.97; 95% CI, 0.36-3.59). Changes in normalized apparent vessel radius did not differ after adjustment (difference, -0.001 × 10-3; q = 0.996). Scan-rescan and reader-agreement ICCs were 0.948-0.994 and 0.941-0.993, respectively. DATA CONCLUSION: At 5 T, 3D PC-MRA detected greater warming-associated increases in nVol and nLen in SSc than controls. Baseline measurements showed good-to-excellent scan-rescan repeatability in controls and excellent reader agreement. TECHNICAL EFFICACY: Stage 3.

articles.title: Perivascular Diffusivity and Periventricular Susceptibility Changes in Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis: A Combined DTI-ALPS and QSM Study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Progressive periventricular damage in multiple sclerosis (MS) has been linked to impaired perivascular clearance and to susceptibility changes attributed to iron deposition and myelin loss. Their relationship is unclear. PURPOSE/HYPOTHESIS: To compare diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) and periventricular quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) between relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) patients and healthy controls; and to evaluate their correlation and relationships with clinical disability (Expanded Disability Status Scale, EDSS). STUDY TYPE: Retrospective case-control study. POPULATION/SUBJECTS: Thirty one patients with RRMS (mean age, 34.6 ± 8.4 years) and 30 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (mean age, 34.2 ± 8.1 years). FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: 1.5 T; Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and multi-echo gradient-echo (GRE) sequences. ASSESSMENT: DTI-ALPS index and periventricular QSM values were measured from manually placed bilateral regions of interest (ROIs). Standardized Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI)-space coordinates were used for DTI-ALPS analysis, and QSM ROIs in periventricular normal-appearing white matter were reviewed by a neuroradiologist. Disability was assessed using the EDSS. STATISTICAL TESTS: Groups were compared using independent-samples t-tests and Cohen's d. Correlations were assessed using Pearson's r, with Spearman's rho as a sensitivity analysis (p < 0.05, two-tailed). RESULTS: DTI-ALPS was lower in MS patients than controls (1.27 ± 0.22 vs. 1.45 ± 0.22; d = 0.828), whereas periventricular QSM was higher (-15.35 ± 4.92 vs. -21.70 ± 6.40 ppb; d = 1.116). A strong negative correlation between the two biomarkers was observed across all subjects (r = -0.738). Both measures correlated with EDSS (DTI-ALPS r = -0.509; QSM r = 0.501) and differed between EDSS subgroups (EDSS > 2.0 vs. ≤ 2.0: DTI-ALPS 1.160 vs. 1.364; QSM -12.33 vs. -17.83 ppb). DATA CONCLUSION: Reduced DTI-ALPS and higher periventricular QSM-derived susceptibility were each moderately associated with disability in RRMS. The negative DTI-ALPS-QSM correlation in both groups indicates an association between perivascular diffusivity, a putative marker of glymphatic function, and periventricular QSM-derived susceptibility; causality cannot be established from this cross-sectional design. STAGE OF TECHNICAL EFFICACY: 2.

articles.title: Automated Cerebrospinal Fluid Flow Quantification in Hydrocephalus Using Phase-Contrast Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
articles.abstract: Quantitative cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow analysis with phase-contrast magnetic resonance imaging depends on segmentation and is affected by operator variability. This cohort method-comparison study evaluated whether a flow-aware deep learning (DL) model provides reproducible C2-C3 CSF segmentation and flow quantification compared with repeated manual segmentation. Ten hydrocephalus patients underwent 3-T phase-contrast magnetic resonance imaging at C2-C3, with 32 magnitude and phase frames across the cardiac cycle. Three experts and one novice segmented each case twice using semi-automatic software, generating 80 manual annotations. A pretrained flow-aware 2D-UNet generated one fixed automatic segmentation per case. The inference pipeline was deterministic, meaning that repeated processing of the same input with fixed model weights and settings produced identical masks. A multi-expert reference was defined as the arithmetic mean of the expert measurements. Region of interest (ROI) surface area, peak flow amplitude, and stroke volume were compared using mean difference, Bland-Altman 95% limits of agreement, Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (CCC), and intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Expert ICC(1,1) was 0.88-0.97 for surface area, 0.97-1.00 for peak flow amplitude, and 0.97-0.99 for stroke volume; novice values were 0.63, 0.95, and 0.92, respectively. Compared with the multi-expert reference, model mean differences were -0.42 mm2 for surface area, -0.00 mL/s for peak flow amplitude, and -0.01 mL for stroke volume, with CCC values of 0.50, 0.87, and 0.86. Bland-Altman limits of agreement were -69.12 to 68.27 mm2, -1.47 to 1.46 mL/s, and -0.34 to 0.31 mL. The model provided rapid, deterministic CSF segmentation with small cohort-level mean differences in peak flow amplitude and stroke volume; however, individual-level agreement with the flow-derived multi-expert reference was lower than for expert and novice segmentations obtained using the semi-automatic workflow.

articles.title: Influence of forehead gap size on eye protection provided by lead eyewear worn over prescription glasses: A Monte Carlo study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Due to exposure to high levels of scattered ionizing radiation, interventional radiology (IR) physicians have an elevated risk of radiation-induced eye injuries and cataracts. Previous studies have evaluated the protective effects of regular lead glasses and recommended measures to improve radiation protection for the eyes. However, the protective effects of fit-over eyewear-lead eyewear worn over prescription glasses-have not been thoroughly examined. Importantly, a previous study noted that the space required to accommodate prescription glasses may reduce eye protection. PURPOSE: Monte Carlo (MC) simulations were performed to quantify the protective effects of fit-over eyewear and assess the relative effectiveness of adding bottom shields to conventional lead eyewear to improve eye protection. METHODS: Conventional lead glasses comprising front and side lenses and prescription glasses with plastic lenses and titanium frames were modeled. Lead glasses with bottom shields were created by bending the lower edges of the front lenses of conventional eyewear without increasing the total lens area. Three lead lens thickness values were tested: 0.07, 0.5, and 0.75 mm. Using a mesh-type reference computational phantom representing an adult male to simulate an IR physician, MC simulations were performed with a transcatheter arterial chemoembolization setup. The Particle and Heavy Ion Transport code system was used to calculate the radiation dose deposited in each eye-sensitive volume. The distance (d) between the forehead and front lead lens varied systematically. Protective effects were evaluated using the shielding rate (%) calculated as: (1-Dpr/D0) × 100, where D0 is the radiation dose without protection and Dpr is the dose with eye protection. RESULTS: For the eye near the X-ray source (left eye), the conventional models showed shielding rates >50% when the lead thickness was 0.5 or 0.75 mm and d was ≤0.5 cm. The conventional 0.07-mm lead eyewear exhibited shielding rates <50% when d was 0.5 cm, and <26% when d was ≥0.8 cm. However, 0.07-mm lead eyewear with bottom shields maintained approximately 50% shielding when d increased to 1.0 cm. The models using 0.5- or 0.75-mm lead lenses with bottom shields exhibited shielding rates >76% at d = 1.0 cm. Notably, the shielding rates for the right eye were <12% regardless of introducing bottom shields. The right eye doses were 45-48% of the left eye lens dose without protection. CONCLUSION: By quantifying the relationship between the size of the lens gap and shielding rates, this study estimates the protective effects of fit-over eyewear and can help IR physicians select suitable eyewear. Our findings show that fit-over eyewear with bottom shields effectively protects the left eye during posterior-anterior projection. Although introducing bottom shields can improve conventional side-shield models in terms of increased shielding rate for the left eye, the shielding rates for the right eye remained low because of the gap around the nose. Further study of new designs with a shielded covering over the nose may be warranted.

articles.title: Low-dose CT denoising using a diffusion prior via score distillation sampling.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) reduces radiation exposure but amplifies noise, which can degrade diagnostic reliability. Recent studies have applied diffusion-based models to LDCT denoising and shown promising performance. However, many of these approaches require paired LDCT and normal-dose CT (NDCT) data or dose-specific retraining, and their reconstruction procedures are often strictly coupled to a predefined diffusion trajectory. PURPOSE: This study proposes an optimization-based LDCT denoising framework that uses a pre-trained NDCT diffusion model as an image prior and can be applied across various dose levels without dose-specific retraining. METHODS: We formulate LDCT denoising as an optimization problem guided by a pre-trained score-based generative model (SGM) trained only on NDCT images. The Poisson data fidelity term enforces consistency with the measured projection data, whereas the score distillation sampling (SDS) term acts as a regularizer that guides the reconstruction toward the NDCT distribution learned by the pre-trained SGM. The denoised image is obtained by iteratively optimizing a projection-domain residual variable using the combined Poisson data fidelity gradient and SDS-based regularization gradient. RESULTS: The proposed method effectively suppressed noise while preserving fine anatomical structures across multiple dose levels using a single pre-trained diffusion model. Quantitative evaluations with respect to full-dose reference images and visual comparisons demonstrated competitive performance compared with supervised and self-supervised LDCT denoising baselines. CONCLUSIONS: The results show that diffusion-based image priors can be leveraged across various low-dose levels within the proposed optimization-based denoising framework. Our work suggests that SDS-guided diffusion priors are a promising direction for LDCT denoising in data-limited settings.

articles.title: Model-based image restoration targeting higher-dose digital mammography: Impact on radiologists' detection of clustered microcalcifications.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Image noise in digital mammography (DM) can obscure image details and reduce the detectability of clinically relevant findings such as microcalcifications. PURPOSE: To present and evaluate an extended model-based (MB) image restoration pipeline for DM that incorporates quantum, electronic, and structural noise components, as well as spatial noise correlation, and to assess its effect on breast radiologists' detection of simulated microcalcification clusters in clinical mammograms. METHODS: A total of 120 clinical DM images acquired using a GE Senographe Pristina system were used. Simulated microcalcification clusters were inserted into locally dense fibroglandular regions at controlled contrast levels. The restoration pipeline was configured to target the signal and noise characteristics predicted by the model for an acquisition at approximately twice the original radiation dose. Six breast radiologists with different levels of experience, classified as Junior or Senior, participated in two human observer experiments: (i) a pilot study using original clinical images with simulated clusters and a four-alternative forced-choice (4AFC) protocol combined with a three-down-one-up (3D1U) staircase to estimate reader-specific contrast detection thresholds and achieve comparable baseline task difficulty across readers; and (ii) a main 4AFC observer study using individualized datasets generated according to each reader's estimated contrast threshold, in which microcalcification detection performance was compared between the original and restored image conditions based on the percentage of correct responses (PC). Two generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) were used: the first evaluated the effect of image condition as a fixed effect, with reader and case as crossed random intercepts, and the second evaluated the effect of reader experience on detection performance in the original image condition. RESULTS: At the reader-specific contrast thresholds estimated in the pilot study, the mean PC for the original images was 78.3%, within the prespecified target performance range. Mean PC increased to 84.3% for the restored images, corresponding to an absolute improvement of 6.0 percentage points. The primary GLMM indicated a significant restoration effect on detection performance (OR = 1.57, 95% CI: 1.15-2.14, p = 0.005  ). Baseline mean PC was 78.7% for Junior readers and 78.0% for Senior readers, and the separate GLMM found no evidence of an experience-group effect under the original image condition ( p = 0.858  ). CONCLUSIONS: The proposed extended MB restoration pipeline improved the detectability of simulated microcalcification clusters by breast radiologists under the controlled 4AFC conditions investigated. By targeting the signal and noise characteristics predicted by the model for an acquisition at approximately twice the original radiation dose without requiring additional radiation exposure, the method represents a promising approach for improving microcalcification detectability in DM.

articles.title: DoseRAD2026: A benchmark dataset for AI-accelerated photon and proton dose calculation in radiotherapy.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Accurate dose calculation is a fundamental component of modern radiotherapy, enabling precise tumor irradiation while sparing surrounding healthy tissue. With the increasing adoption of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-guided radiotherapy and growing interest in real-time adaptive radiotherapy, there is a demand for fast and accurate dose calculation techniques on both computed tomography (CT) and MRI. To facilitate research in this area, the DoseRAD2026 dataset and accompanying challenge introduce a publicly available benchmark dataset comprising paired CT and MRI data with corresponding beam-level photon and proton Monte Carlo (MC) dose distributions, enabling the development and systematic evaluation of advanced dose calculation and prediction methods. ACQUISITION AND VALIDATION METHODS: The DoseRAD2026 dataset comprises paired CT and MRI data from 115 patients (75 training, 40 testing) treated on a hybrid MRI-linear accelerator (MRI-linac) for thoracic or abdominal lesions and is derived from the SynthRAD2025 dataset. Image pre-processing included deformable image registration, air-cavity correction and resampling. Ground-truth photon (6 MV) and proton dose distributions were generated using open-source MC dose calculation algorithms and resulted in a training dataset of 40,500 photon beams and 81,000 proton beamlets. DATA FORMAT AND USAGE NOTES: The dataset is organized into photon and proton subsets, each comprising paired CT-MRI images, beam-level dose distributions, and JSON files specifying patient-specific beam configurations. Data are provided in compressed MetaImage (.mha) format with standardized naming linking dose files to beam parameters in the JSON files. The dataset is released under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license, with the training set available from April 2026 and the test set withheld until March 2030. POTENTIAL APPLICATIONS: The DoseRAD2026 dataset enables benchmarking and development of fast dose calculation methods for radiotherapy applications. Potential use cases include rapid beam-level dose estimation for photon and proton therapy, MRI-based dose calculation in MRI-only and MRI-guided radiotherapy workflows, and support for real-time adaptive radiotherapy strategies.

articles.title: Uncertainty-aware hybrid model for reliable navigation guidance in prostate biopsy.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Prostate biopsy - performed under ultrasound (US) guidance - is the only confirmatory procedure for diagnosing prostate cancer. If several systems aiming at improving the accuracy of tissue sampling for histopathological analysis exist, they often fail to adequately account for patient / tissue motion and deformation during the procedure or are not suitable for real-time guidance towards a pre-defined target. PURPOSE: This work proposes a real-time assistance method to help urologists navigate between biopsy sites leveraging both 2D US and 3D US information. METHODS: The proposed hybrid framework combines three ResNet-18-based sub-networks with a Kalman filter to track the pose of the current 2D US frame within a reference 3D US volume acquired during the intervention. Two of the networks predict relative rigid transformations from pairs of US frames or frame/slice combinations extracted from the 3D volume. A third network predicts the registration error from a frame/slice pair and acts as a large-error detector. This error prediction module is integrated directly into the iterative registration process, to ensure robust tracking in the presence of tissue deformation or image artifacts, while also providing an uncertainty estimate of registration quality at each time step. The proposed framework was trained and evaluated on complex biopsy trajectories generated from a dataset of 847 3D US volumes acquired during real transrectal prostate biopsy procedures from 97 patients. The dataset was divided into training (78 patients, 669 volumes), validation (10 patients, 115 volumes), and test (9 patients, 63 volumes) sets. Performance was compared with an image-correlation-based baseline method using clinically relevant evaluation metrics, including the mean surface registration error (mean SRE) over 25-s trajectories, as well as the percentage of registered frames with an SRE below 2.5 mm and 5 mm. Statistical significance was assessed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (adjusted with Holm-Bonferroni correction) and 95% confidence bootstrap intervals (CI 95%) across the test cohort. Effect sizes were quantified with rank-biserial correlation (RBC). RESULTS: Compared with the baseline method, the proposed approach achieved a significant reduction in the mean SRE over 25-s trajectories, decreasing from 3.1  [ 2.2 , 4.9 ]  to 2.2  [ 1.8 , 2.5 ]   mm (median [CI 95%], p = 0.016, RBC = 0.96). In addition, the proposed large-error detector - used for uncertainty estimation - achieved a balanced accuracy score of 0.81 for classifying registration errors above or below a given threshold of 5 mm. CONCLUSIONS: These results demonstrate the potential of the proposed framework to improve the accuracy and robustness of real-time prostate biopsy navigation guidance.

articles.title: Intravenous oxycodone versus morphine patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) after uterine artery embolisation: A propensity matched case-control study.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: The use of intravenous oxycodone is still limited in the Interventional Radiology setting. This study aimed to assess the safety and efficacy of intravenous oxycodone used in patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) after uterine fibroid embolisation (UFE), compared to morphine. METHODS: Retrospective case-control study. The study group consisted of patients treated with UFE between March and December 2024, using an oxycodone protocol. The control group consisted of a previously published dataset using morphine protocol. Primary outcomes were safety and the incidence of severe nausea. RESULTS: There were 57 patients in the oxycodone group compared to 69 in the morphine group. After propensity score matching, this left 43 in the oxycodone group and 60 in the morphine group. Groups were similar in terms of background demographics, however the use of smaller 355-500 micrometre polyvinyl alcohol particles were higher in the oxycodone group (100% vs 18%, p < 0.001).No analgesic-related adverse events were observed in either group. The incidence of severe nausea was lower in the oxycodone group (43.3% vs 37.2%, p = 0.533) despite a higher rate of post-embolisation syndrome (65.1% vs 48.3%, p = 0.091). After multiparametric logistic regression, oxycodone was associated with a 64% reduced odds of severe nausea (OR 0.36, p = 0.217). CONCLUSIONS: Intravenous oxycodone PCA is safe and showed a trend towards a lower incidence of severe nausea compared with morphine PCA. ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: There is limited evidence of the use of oxycodone PCA to treat post-embolisation syndrome. This study showed it was safe and resulted in reduced nausea compared to morphine.

articles.title: From Isolated Intelligence to Interpretive Infrastructure in Radiology AI.
articles.abstract: Radiology has more regulatory-cleared artificial intelligence tools than any other medical specialty, yet they have delivered less consistent clinical impact than their benchmark performance suggested. We argue that the dominant response, scaling perceptual models and extending them toward autonomous agency, mistakes the nature of the problem. The limitation is architectural, not algorithmic: current systems perform isolated perception while remaining disconnected from the temporal, contextual, and experiential integration that interpretation requires. We trace this to a fundamental simulation gap, the absence of the counterfactual signal that lets AI reach superhuman performance in other domains, and argue that scaling alone cannot close it. In response, we outline a hybrid orchestration layer, grounded in established clinical frameworks, that assembles a comprehensive evidence base for the radiologist while keeping generative components constrained and interpretive judgment human. The shift is one of design paradigm: from isolated tools deployed alongside the radiologist to interpretive infrastructure that composes validated outputs into coherent evidence without anchoring the reader's own assessment.

articles.title: The b-Value Dependence for Higher-Degree Spherical Harmonic Powers of the Diffusion MRI Signal Follows Stick Model Predictions in White Matter.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To compare the dependence on b-value of the spherical harmonic powers for the diffusion MRI signal in white matter to theoretical predictions from the stick model of water diffusion within axons. METHODS: Diffusion MRI data were acquired at 3 T in three healthy adults with 10 b-value shells (b = 1000-10 000 s/mm2) and 64 directions per shell. For every b-value, the signal was expanded in spherical harmonics for all even degrees l up to l = 6, and the harmonic power for each degree was calculated. These were compared in selected white matter regions of interest to the theoretical predictions of the stick model, which depend on just two adjustable parameters: the intra-axonal diffusivity and an amplitude factor for each degree. The intra-axonal diffusivity was estimated independently using triple diffusion encoding MRI, leaving the amplitude factor as the sole fitting parameter. RESULTS: Close agreement between experiment and theory was found for b  ≳   4000 s/mm2, the threshold where extra-axonal water signal is expected to be strongly suppressed, for total cerebral white matter as well as separately within the genu, body, and splenium of the corpus callosum. These findings extend prior studies that either considered only the l = 0 harmonic power or treated the intra-axonal diffusivity as a fitting parameter. CONCLUSION: In white matter, the b-value dependence of the diffusion MRI signal's even degree spherical harmonic powers up to l = 6 are relatively well-described by the stick model of axons for b  ≳   4000 s/mm2.

articles.title: Camera calibration and tracking for augmented reality during robotic surgery.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Robot-assisted surgery (RAS) offers clinical advantages but remains limited by reduced visualization and lack of tactile feedback. Augmented reality (AR), achieved by overlaying preoperative imaging onto laparoscopic video, may mitigate these challenges. This study evaluates the accuracy and clinical feasibility of an AR system that uses electromagnetic (EM) tracking to determine the position of the robotic endoscope and enable real-time image overlay during surgery. METHODS: For calibration, an EM sensor was rigidly attached to the robotic endoscope and a second sensor to a calibration checkerboard. 35 calibration images were acquired. To determine the required number of calibration images, 2600 random subsets containing 5-30 images were calibrated using RANSAC-based robust estimation and evaluated on 16 separately recorded checkerboard frames using three-dimensional (3D) Euclidean error. Subsequently, a clinically suitable adapter carrying the EM tracker was rigidly mounted on the robotic endoscope and evaluated during 16 robot-assisted pelvic lymph node dissection (RPLND) procedures. RESULTS: Calibration accuracy and robustness improved with increasing dataset size. A dataset of 19 images was the smallest dataset size with a median 3D error within 5% of the best observed performance, with a mean 3D Euclidean error of 0.541 ± 0.060 mm. Using the same protocol, the clinical adapter achieved 0.784 ± 0.075 mm. System evaluation during 16 RPLND provided stable, real-time tracking and AR visualization. CONCLUSION: The proposed calibration and tracking approach enables sub-millimeter AR overlay accuracy while allowing continuous tracking of the robotic endoscope through an externally mounted EM tracker. Its successful use during 16 RPLND procedures demonstrates that the method can be integrated into a clinical robotic workflow and supports real-time visualization without substantial procedural modification. These findings provide a technical foundation for further development and validation of image-guided AR applications in robotic-assisted surgery.
articles.journal: Int J Comput Assist Radiol Surg

articles.title: AI-based automated body composition analysis from whole-body MRI and (PET-) CT: an intermodal comparison from same-day examinations.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: To determine intermodal agreement of AI-derived volumetric body composition metrics between [18 F]FDG-PET/CT-derived low-dose CT and whole-body MRI (wb-MRI). METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed same-day whole-body low-dose CT, obtained from [18F]FDG-PET/CT, and wb-MRI from consecutive multiple myeloma patients from the prospective GMMG-HD7- and GMMG-HD8-/DSMM-XIX-trials. An automated deep learning pipeline based on the TotalSegmentator model, and its MRI variant were used to segment skeletal muscle (SM), subcutaneous- (SAT) and abdominal visceral adipose tissue (VAT) from CT and MRI, respectively. Volumetric measures and single-slice estimates were derived. Agreement between CT- and MRI-based metrics was assessed using Pearson r, intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), and Bland-Altman analyses. RESULTS: Forty-two multiple myeloma patients with same-day PET/CT and wb-MRI were included. For AI-based volumetric body composition metrics, CT and MRI demonstrated high agreement (ICC > 0.95) across all SM, SAT and VAT. However, Bland-Altmann plots revealed systematic modality-related differences between MRI and CT: both SM (bias: -2582 ml, p < 0.0001) and VAT (bias: -211 ml, p < 0.0001) were significantly lower when extracted from MRI compared to CT, while for SAT, the difference was not statistically significant (bias: -263 ml, p = 0.1629). For AI-based single slice analysis, agreement remained high for SAT and VAT (ICC > 0.97), while being lower for SM (ICC 0.87). Bland-Altman plots showed that SM was systematically and significantly lower when obtained from MRI than from CT (bias: -18.4cm2, p < 0.0001). CONCLUSIONS: Automated body composition measures from (PET-)CT and wb-MRI are highly concordant but show consistent intermodal biases that should be considered when pooling multimodal data or applying modality-agnostic thresholds. CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

articles.title: Assessing Calcified Coronary Lesions to Guide Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: From Angiography to Intracoronary Imaging.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Coronary artery calcification is a leading cause of stent failure and a strong predictor of adverse outcomes after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Accurate characterization of calcium burden, depth, and morphology is central to procedural planning, targeted treatment, and better outcomes. This review summarizes the contemporary armamentarium for imaging calcified coronary lesions, from coronary angiography and computed tomography to advanced intracoronary imaging, and how it facilitates treatment. Methods: We synthesized evidence from landmark studies, validated imaging scoring systems, registries, and current guideline and consensus documents addressing the assessment and imaging-guided treatment of coronary calcification. Results: Invasive angiography shows poor diagnostic accuracy for coronary calcium detection, characterization, and quantification. Coronary CT angiography noninvasively quantifies calcium (Agatston score and three-dimensional volume) and supports preprocedural planning, although it may overestimate calcium volume. Intravascular imaging by means of intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) and optical coherence tomography (OCT) effectively detects coronary calcium. Their use is associated with improved clinical outcomes compared with sole angiographic guidance. The addition of near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS-IVUS) characterizes lipids within calcified plaque and high-risk calcified nodules. OCT provides the highest spatial resolution and uniquely measures calcium thickness and longitudinal calcium length, while the utilization of artificial intelligence further enhances calcium assessment. Integration of these modalities into a morphology-based, imaging-guided approach facilitates calcium detection and modification and supports PCI optimization. Conclusions: Intravascular imaging, along with coronary CT angiography, has transformed the assessment of calcified coronary lesions. Combining their strengths enables precise, lesion-specific preparation; randomized trials show that intravascular imaging guidance improves outcomes in complex PCI, while CT-guided PCI planning is emerging as a complementary strategy whose clinical value is now being tested in randomized trials.

articles.title: Cardiac Computed Tomography in Infective Endocarditis: A Radiological Perspective on Structural Complications and Emerging Diagnostic Technologies.
articles.abstract: Background: Infective endocarditis (IE) remains a life-threatening disease associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography are the first-line imaging modalities, but their diagnostic performance may be reduced in patients with prosthetic valves, intracardiac devices, previous cardiac surgery, extensive calcification, or suspected periannular extension. Cardiac computed tomography (CT) provides complementary high-resolution anatomical information and has gained increasing importance within contemporary multimodality diagnostic pathways. Scope: This Review critically examines the current role of cardiac CT in IE, including acquisition and reconstruction strategies, lesion-specific imaging findings, applications in native, prosthetic, transcatheter, and device-related infection, extracardiac assessment, and preoperative planning. Comparative observations regarding echocardiography and selected multimodality techniques are integrated where directly relevant. Emerging applications of spectral CT, photon-counting detector CT, deep learning reconstruction, radiomics, and artificial intelligence are appraised according to four levels of evidence: clinically validated IE applications, preliminary IE-specific evidence, indirect cardiovascular evidence, and conceptual applications. Main Findings: Cardiac CT is particularly valuable for detecting and anatomically characterizing periannular complications, including abscesses, pseudoaneurysms, fistulous tracts, inflammatory extension, and prosthetic dehiscence. Multiphase electrocardiography (ECG)-gated acquisition improves the assessment of dynamic valvular and prosthetic abnormalities. Transesophageal echocardiography remains more sensitive for small or highly mobile vegetations, leaflet perforation, regurgitant jets, and intracardiac flow abnormalities, demonstrating that the two techniques are complementary rather than interchangeable. Cardiac CT also contributes to coronary assessment, surgical planning, evaluation of previous grafts and reconstructive material, and selected extracardiac complications. Conclusions: Cardiac CT is an important component of contemporary multimodality IE assessment, but it should not be regarded as a replacement for echocardiography. Its clinical value depends on the infected substrate, suspected complication, acquisition protocol, and integration with echocardiographic, microbiological, surgical, and clinical findings. Emerging technologies may improve image quality and quantitative characterization, but most remain supported by preliminary IE-specific, indirect cardiovascular, or conceptual evidence and should not yet be considered established IE-specific diagnostic tools.

articles.title: Low-Dose CT in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Techniques, Evidence, and Clinical Impact.
articles.abstract: Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) is essential for reducing potential radiation-associated risks, but increased noise and artifacts can compromise diagnostic confidence. This review examines how AI is reshaping LDCT by improving reconstruction, denoising, protocol optimization, and workflow integration. It outlines the evolution from FBP to IR and then to deep learning methods that better preserve anatomical detail while reducing noise. The review also considers emerging applications in photon-counting CT (PCCT) and discusses clinical use in screening, pediatric imaging, oncology, cardiac imaging, and emergency care. These developments may support safer imaging, improve consistency across studies, and reduce the need for repeat examinations. However, important challenges remain, including limited generalizability across scanners and patient populations, the potential loss of subtle findings, changes in quantitative imaging features, and the need for careful validation before widespread clinical adoption. Further research should focus on multicenter validation, task-based performance assessment, and integration into routine clinical workflows.

articles.title: Role of facet tropism in lumbar spine pathologies: Facet osteoarthritis, degenerative disc disease and ligamentum flavum thickness.
articles.abstract: Facet tropism (FT), defined as asymmetry in the orientation of the bilateral facet joints, may alter segmental biomechanics and load distribution in the lumbar spine. Our aim is to investigate the possible relationship between FT and degenerative disc disease (DDD), facet joint osteoarthritis (FJOA), and ligamentum flavum thickening (LFT) in the LS. A total of 279 patients aged 40-70 years who underwent lumbar MRI were retrospectively analyzed. Facet joint angles were measured on axial T2-weighted images at the L3-4, L4-5, and L5-S1 levels and FT was defined as an inter-facet angle difference of ≥7°. DDD was graded using the modified Pfirrmann scale, FJOA using the Weishaupt classification and LFT was measured directly on axial images. FT was detected at least at one level in 50.5% of patients. In the presence of tropism, modified Pfirrmann and Weishaupt scores were significantly higher at the L4-5 and L5-S1 levels, and LFT was significantly greater at the L3-4 and L4-5 levels (p < 0.05). Age and FJOA had significant effects on DDD, whereas the independent impact of tropism was significant only at certain levels. MANOVA showed that the overall multivariate effect of FT on degenerative parameters was not statistically significant. FT was more frequently observed at lower lumbar levels and was associated with certain degenerative changes. However, due to the multifactorial nature of spinal degenerative changes, FT alone was not found to be a decisive determinant.
